overview:
Rishabha (Ṛṣabha) appears in a range of non-Jain Sanskrit sources, most prominently in Vedic and Purāṇic literature, where the term carries both lexical and theological meanings. In early Vedic texts such as the Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda, ṛṣabha primarily denotes a "bull," "male animal," or "the most excellent one," and functions as an epithet rather than a clearly individuated religious figure. In these contexts, the word can be applied to deities like Rudra or Indra, or used metaphorically for power, sovereignty, and excellence, without explicit narrative connection to the Jain Tirthankara R̥ṣabhanātha.

By the classical and Purāṇic period, Rishabha is incorporated into Hindu narrative theology, especially within Vaiṣṇava and sometimes Śaiva frameworks. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa present Rishabha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu, born to King Nābhi and Queen Merudevī (or Sudevī in some recensions), ruling as a dharmic king and later renouncing the world to become an extreme ascetic (avadhūta). These accounts parallel several motifs found in Jain hagiographies of R̥ṣabhanātha—such as kingship, renunciation, and the son Bharata—but they are embedded in a distinct theological system where Rishabha is explicitly a manifestation of Viṣṇu and a teacher of bhakti-inflected dharma.

Scholars of comparative religion have noted that the Purāṇic Rishabha narrative likely reflects a process of mutual appropriation and reinterpretation between Jain and Hindu communities in regions where both traditions were influential. Some modern authors, following Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan and others, argue that certain Yajurvedic and Purāṇic references presuppose a figure close to the Jain Tirthankara, while other philological studies caution that many early occurrences of ṛṣabha are purely lexical and not securely tied to any historical or sectarian personage. As a result, the relationship between the Vedic "ṛṣabha" as a term of excellence, the Purāṇic avatāra Rishabha, and the Jain Tirthankara R̥ṣabhanātha remains a debated field of interpretation.

In non-Jain texts, then, Rishabha occupies a spectrum: from a poetic epithet in the Vedas, to a fully narrativized avatāra in the Bhāgavata and Viṣṇu Purāṇas, to a figure occasionally assimilated into Śaiva discourse (for example, in later Purāṇas that associate his bull-symbol and mountain nirvāṇa place with Śiva). These sources do not function as Jain canonical authority, but they are crucial for understanding how R̥ṣabhanātha was perceived, reimagined, or contested in broader Indian religious literature, and how Jain and non-Jain communities negotiated shared mythic figures over time.

primary_sources.title: Ṛgveda 10.166
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vedic seers (ṛṣis), no single author
primary_sources.original_text:
ऋषभं मा समानानां सपत्नानां विषासहिम् ।
हन्तारं शत्रूणां कृधि विराजं गोपतिं गवाम् ॥१॥
अहमस्मि सपत्नहेन्द्र इवारिष्टो अक्षतः ।
अधः सपत्ना मे पदोरिमे सर्वे अभिष्ठिताः ॥२॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṛṣabhaṁ mā samānānāṁ sapatnānāṁ viṣāsahim |
hantāraṁ śatrūṇāṁ kṛdhi virājaṁ gopatiṁ gavām ||1||
aham asmi sapatna-hendra ivāriṣṭo akṣataḥ |
adhaḥ sapatnā me pador ime sarve abhiṣṭhitāḥ ||2||
primary_sources.translation:
1. Make me a bull among my peers, a conqueror of rivals; make me the slayer of my foes, a shining lord, protector of the cattle.
2. I am the slayer of my rivals, like Indra, unwounded and unharmed; all these enemies of mine are cast down beneath my feet.
primary_sources.notes: In this hymn, ṛṣabha is used as a metaphorical epithet—"bull" and "most excellent"—for power and sovereignty. The term does not clearly denote a distinct religious figure, but rather functions as a poetic image applied to the speaker and associated deities such as Indra. Later Jain and Hindu traditions sometimes retrospectively read such occurrences as hints of R̥ṣabhanātha, yet philologically the passage is best understood as lexical and metaphorical, not as a biographical reference.

primary_sources.title: Atharvaveda 9.4.14–15 (selected lines)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vedic seers (ṛṣis), no single author
primary_sources.notes: Atharvavedic passages use ṛṣabha in the sense of a powerful bull or an excellent male, sometimes in ritual or medicinal contexts. The word can also denote a kind of medicinal plant in certain lists. These usages reinforce the semantic field of strength and excellence, but they do not provide narrative material about a person named Rishabha. Later identifications with the Jain Tirthankara or the Purāṇic avatāra are therefore interpretive overlays rather than explicit in the Atharvaveda itself.

primary_sources.title: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.5.13 (indicative reference)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vedic ritualists, no single author
primary_sources.notes: In the Brāhmaṇa literature, ṛṣabha again appears as an epithet—"bull among the gods"—marking preeminence and ritual potency. Some modern writers cite such passages to argue for an early cult of Rishabha as a distinct figure, but the text itself presents the term as a qualitative description rather than a personal name with biography. This illustrates the methodological difficulty of moving from lexical occurrences to historical or sectarian identifications.

primary_sources.title: Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Skandha 5, chapters 3–6 (example verse 5.4.1)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa; compiled and redacted over time
primary_sources.original_text: नाभेः पत्न्यां मेरुदेव्याṁ भगवान् ऋषभो नामासीत् यः स्वांशेनावतीर्णो लोकानां स्वधर्मोपदेशेन।
primary_sources.transliteration: nābheḥ patnyāṁ merudevyāṁ bhagavān ṛṣabho nāmāsīt yaḥ svāṁśenāvatīrṇo lokānāṁ sva-dharmopadeśena.
primary_sources.translation: To the wife of King Nābhi, Merudevī, the Blessed Lord descended in his own portion as Rishabha by name, in order to instruct the people in their own dharma.
primary_sources.notes: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa offers the most detailed non-Jain narrative of Rishabha, portraying him as a partial avatāra of Viṣṇu. He is born to King Nābhi and Queen Merudevī, rules as a righteous king, fathers one hundred sons (including Bharata), and eventually renounces the kingdom to live as an avadhūta, exemplifying extreme asceticism and inner equanimity. Many motifs—royal birth, renunciation, son Bharata—parallel Jain accounts of R̥ṣabhanātha, but the theological frame is explicitly Vaiṣṇava: Rishabha is Bhagavān, a manifestation of Viṣṇu, and his teaching is integrated into bhakti and Purāṇic cosmology. Some scholars see this as a conscious appropriation of a Jain figure into a Hindu avatāra list; others argue for a shared, regionally circulating mythic complex that both traditions shaped in different ways.

primary_sources.title: Viṣṇu Purāṇa (book 2, genealogical sections, indicative verse)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa; compiled and redacted over time
primary_sources.original_text: नाभेः पुत्रो ऋषभो नाम राजर्षिर् धर्मवित्। तस्य पुत्रो भरतो यस्माद् भारतं वरं वरम्।
primary_sources.transliteration:
nābheḥ putro ṛṣabho nāma rājarṣir dharmavit |
tasya putro bharato yasmād bhārataṁ varaṁ varam.
primary_sources.translation: Nābhi’s son was the royal sage named Rishabha, knower of dharma. His son was Bharata, from whom the land came to be called Bhārata.
primary_sources.notes: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa briefly mentions Rishabha in royal genealogies, identifying him as a righteous king and father of Bharata. In some recensions and commentarial traditions, he is also counted among Viṣṇu’s avatāras, though the narrative detail is far less extensive than in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. The association of Bharata and the naming of Bhārata-varṣa parallels Jain traditions that link R̥ṣabhanātha’s son Bharata to the naming of the land, illustrating a shared mythic motif across sectarian boundaries.

primary_sources.title: Later Śaiva Purāṇic references (e.g., Liṅga Purāṇa, summary)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa; Śaiva redactors over time
primary_sources.translation: … Rishabhadeva is described as an avatāra of Nīlakaṇṭha (Śiva), endowed with the characteristics of the bull …
primary_sources.notes: Some later Śaiva Purāṇas and sectarian texts appropriate Rishabhadeva into a Śaiva framework, emphasizing his bull-symbol (vṛṣabha) and mountain nirvāṇa place, and aligning him with Śiva’s iconography and epithets. These passages are not uniform across manuscripts and often reflect regional or sectarian reinterpretations. They show how a figure associated with Jainism and Vaiṣṇavism could also be drawn into Śaiva discourse, further complicating the cross-traditional identity of Rishabha in non-Jain literature.

misconceptions.myth: Every occurrence of the word "ṛṣabha" in Vedic literature refers directly to the Jain Tirthankara R̥ṣabhanātha.
misconceptions.reality: In the Ṛgveda, Atharvaveda, and Brāhmaṇa texts, "ṛṣabha" most often functions as a common noun or epithet meaning "bull," "male animal," or "most excellent one." These passages lack the biographical and doctrinal markers that would securely identify a specific Tirthankara. While later Jain and Hindu interpreters sometimes read these occurrences as hints of R̥ṣabhanātha, philological analysis shows that the primary sense is lexical and metaphorical, not a personal name with a developed religious narrative.

misconceptions.myth: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa simply reproduces Jain doctrine and can be treated as a Jain canonical source on R̥ṣabhanātha.
misconceptions.reality: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa presents Rishabha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu within a distinctly Vaiṣṇava theological framework. Although its narrative shares motifs with Jain hagiography—such as royal birth, renunciation, and the son Bharata—it integrates these into Purāṇic cosmology, bhakti theology, and a list of Viṣṇu’s incarnations. It is therefore a non-Jain text that reinterprets a possibly shared or borrowed figure, not a Jain canonical authority. Using it as a direct doctrinal source for Jain practice or belief requires careful comparison with Jain āgamas and commentaries and, in traditional settings, guidance from qualified Jain teachers.

misconceptions.myth: There is unanimous scholarly agreement that Vedic and Purāṇic Rishabha are historically identical to the Jain Tirthankara, proving a single, continuous cult from the Vedic age.
misconceptions.reality: Modern scholarship is divided. Some authors, including Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan and later comparative religion scholars, argue that certain Yajurvedic and Purāṇic references presuppose a figure closely related to the Jain R̥ṣabhanātha and that cross-traditional borrowing occurred early. Other philologists and historians caution that many Vedic occurrences of "ṛṣabha" are purely lexical, and that Purāṇic narratives may reflect later sectarian appropriation rather than direct continuity from the Vedic period. As a result, the identification of all non-Jain Rishabha references with the Jain Tirthankara remains a matter of interpretation and debate, not an established historical fact.
